newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambians vote in marred election.
newsitem.headline: Zambians vote in marred election.

text.p: Zambians queued up to vote on Monday in presidential and parliamentary elections boycotted by the main opposition.
Opponents say that President Frederick Chiluba, who ousted Kenneth Kaunda in 1991 on a free-market and democracy platform, has rigged the polls so that his bid for a second term canot fail.
Chiluba, set for a clear victory after shutting his main rival Kaunda out of the race, called for calm in the election, which has raised political tension in usually tranquil Zambia.
"Let me take this opportunity to appeal to all Zambians to be peaceful during the forthcoming elections," he said in an address carried in government-owned newspapers on Monday.

There were no early reports of any repeat of last week's anti-Chiluba riots by students. Polls opened at dawn and were due to close at five p.m. (1500 GMT). Final results were expected on Tuesday or Wednesday.
The lines at polling stations in the rain-soaked capital Lusaka were due more to the creeping pace of voting than to the weight of people trying to cast their ballots.

Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP) and six smaller opposition groups have called for voters to stay away from the polls, in which Chiluba faces four lesser-known rivals for president. None are seen as having any chance.

The boycott came after Chiluba's Movement for Multi-party Democracy (MMD), which won 125 of the 150 seats in parliament in the 1991 elections, changed the constitution to bar presidential candidates whose parents were born abroad. Kaunda's came from Malawi.

The opposition, which depicts the election as a farce, was hoping for the lowest possible turnout and was aided by Monday's downpours, in addition to a flawed voter registration system which left three-quarters of the 4.6 million adult population without voting cards.
Several UNIP officials were arrested at the weekend for collecting cards from potential voters as part of the campaign to ensure a boycott.
The polls, the second since socialist-oriented Kaunda abandoned one-party rule, were meant to cement democracy in a model African state, but showed instead how optimism can fade.
Foreign donors froze vital aid to the debt-ridden southern African country in protest at the constitutional change.

They said it was clearly aimed at 72-year-old Kaunda, one of Africa's fathers of independence and Cold-War era giants who fell from grace as the economy, potentially rich from copper and agriculture, imploded under 27 years of his rule.

The donors face a dilemma. If they block aid, they will bring new hardship to people already reeling from austerity measures as Chiluba pursues free-market policies and privatisation that have impressed the World Bank.
If they quietly resume it, admitting Chiluba could defy them and win, it will be seen as a blow to democracy.
Political analysts said Chiluba, 53, would have won anyway even if he had let Kaunda stand.
Kaunda has called for civil disobedience and hopes a low turnout will lead to fresh and fairer elections, but analysts said he had little hope of a re-run.
